meta.title: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
meta.description: Compare lunar landing sites and dates: where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon.
app.name: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
app.status: Work in progress during the event weekend (14–15 November 2026). Built so far: the comparison below, with the time remaining before sunset or Earthset, the duration of sunlight and Earth visibility windows.
footer.si: Built with SI (Claude Code, Anthropic) on the author's instructions.
tool.heading: Compare landing sites and dates
tool.intro: Pick a landing site and a date and time (UTC). Each scenario shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon. Sun above the horizon: solar power generation is possible. Earth above the horizon: direct-to-Earth communication is possible.
tool.data_label: Sun and Earth positions: precomputed from JPL Horizons (NASA JPL). Horizon: local terrain from LRO LOLA where the south polar elevation grids used here cover the site; elsewhere an ideal sphere horizon. Each scenario says which one it uses. Own coordinates: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons.
scenario.label: Scenario {n}
glance.heading: Side by side
glance.intro: The same numbers as the scenario cards below, one column per scenario.
comm.no: No direct line of sight to Earth
time.sun.no_set: No sunset before the end of the data ({end} UTC)
time.sun.no_rise: No sunrise before the end of the data ({end} UTC)
time.earth.no_set: No Earthset before the end of the data ({end} UTC)
time.earth.no_rise: No Earthrise before the end of the data ({end} UTC)
sky.aria: Horizon panorama. Sun: azimuth {saz}°, elevation {sel}°. Earth: azimuth {eaz}°, elevation {eel}°.
sky.terrain: Solid line = terrain skyline (LRO LOLA); dashed = ideal sphere horizon
horizon.terrain: Horizon: local terrain from LRO LOLA elevation data.
horizon.sphere: Horizon: ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not included (this site is outside the LOLA south polar grids used here).
details.data: Positions are read from an hourly JPL Horizons table computed for this site (observer on the lunar surface) and linearly interpolated between hours.
details.horizon: Above the horizon means elevation greater than {threshold}° against an ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not included for this site: it lies outside the LRO LOLA south polar elevation grids used here (75°S to the pole).
details.horizon_terrain: Above the horizon means the elevation is more than {threshold}° above the terrain skyline in that direction. The skyline is computed from LRO LOLA south polar elevation grids (80 m and 240 m per pixel) for an observer {h} m above the surface, measured from the same ideal-sphere reference as the JPL Horizons angles. Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset use this skyline.
details.scale: Panorama: azimuth 0–360° left to right; elevation ±{scale}°, the same scale on every scenario.
details.windows: Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset are where the interpolated elevation crosses the horizon threshold. A window that runs past the start or end of the precomputed table is shown as "at least" that long.
state.out_of_range: No precomputed data for this time. Available: {start} to {end} UTC.
state.load_error: Could not load the data for this site.

val.title: Validation — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
val.description: How closely the Sun and Earth angles shown by this tool match JPL Horizons.
val.heading: Validation
val.intro: Do the angles this tool shows match JPL Horizons? Site-and-time pairs were drawn at random (fixed seed), never on a table hour, so they test the hourly interpolation. For each pair, the angles shown by this tool's own code are compared with JPL Horizons asked directly for the same site and minute.
val.not_checked: Terrain horizon: checked below against an independent NASA product (average Sun and Earth visibility maps).
val.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/validate.py (random seed {seed}). Source file: data/validation.json.
val.pgda.heading: Terrain horizon against NASA PGDA
val.pgda.intro: The terrain skyline is checked against an independent NASA product: the average Sun and Earth visibility maps of the lunar south pole (E. Mazarico, NASA GSFC PGDA; LOLA grid, {m} m per pixel). A map value is the share of hourly steps over 18.6 years when any part of the Sun or Earth disc was visible. This tool's value is the share of hours in its own table ({start} to {stop} UTC) when any part of the disc is above its terrain skyline. The periods differ, so the numbers are not expected to match exactly.
val.pgda.window: PGDA range nearby = lowest and highest map value in the {n} × {n} pixels around the point; it shows how fast the value changes within a few hundred metres.
val.pgda.source: Source: NASA GSFC PGDA, Lunar Polar Illumination
val.pgda.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/pgda.py. Source file: data/validation.json.
tl.heading: One lunar day
tl.intro: Sun and Earth elevation above the horizon over 29.5 Earth days around the chosen time (one lunar day). Lines above the horizon line = in view. The bars under the chart mark when each one is in view.
tl.lanes: Upper bar: Sun in view · lower bar: Earth in view
tl.aria: Timeline from {from} to {to} UTC. Sun above the horizon {sun}% of the time, Earth above the horizon {earth}% of the time. Vertical scale ±{scale}°.
custom.hint: Decimal degrees: latitude {latMin} to {latMax} (south is negative); west longitudes may be typed as negative numbers. Computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons; ideal sphere horizon only.
custom.name: Own point ({lat}°, {lon}° E)
custom.invalid.lat: Latitude must be a number from {min}° to {max}°.
custom.invalid.lon: Longitude must be a number from {min}° to {max}° (east positive).
custom.computing: Computing Sun and Earth positions in your browser…
horizon.custom: Horizon: ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not computed for own coordinates.
details.data_custom: Positions are computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons: Astronomy Engine (MIT license) gives the Sun and Earth directions and the Moon's IAU rotation model on an hourly grid over the same dates as the precomputed tables, linearly interpolated between hours. The measured differences from JPL Horizons are on the Validation page.
details.horizon_custom: Above the horizon means elevation greater than {threshold}° against an ideal sphere horizon (radius {r} km). Local terrain is not computed for own coordinates, even inside the LRO LOLA grids.
val.engine.heading: Own coordinates: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons
val.engine.intro: For own coordinates the page computes the Sun and Earth angles itself (Astronomy Engine) on the same hourly grid and interpolates them the same way. The engine was run at the listed-site pairs above and at {n} unnamed check points (not landing sites) spread over the near side, far side and both poles, and compared with JPL Horizons asked directly.
val.engine.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/validate.py --engine (random seed {seed}). Source file: data/validation.json.
shift.heading: Small shifts in location or date
shift.intro: The same two answers when the time moves a little, or the point moves {km} km. Numbers = degrees above (+) or below (−) the horizon used for this scenario.
shift.changed: {n} of {total} shifts change at least one answer.
shift.place_computing: Computing the nearby points in your browser…
shift.place_source: Nearby points: terrain horizon from LRO LOLA (same method as this site). Sun and Earth positions there: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons.
shift.place_none: Location shifts are shown where a LOLA terrain horizon exists. On the ideal sphere, moving {km} km tilts the horizon by only {deg}°.
shift.place_error: Nearby points could not be computed.
